caption.text:
We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image.

The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away.

Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos!

Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center
Producer: Paul Morris

caption.text:
From simple beginnings to the complex universe we know today 💫

Webb has opened a world of opportunity in studying the early universe and galaxy evolution over time. With its advanced infrared instruments, we’re able to see earlier galaxies than ever before. 

This year at the @space_telescopes 2026 symposium, astronomers discussed the chemical simplicity of the early universe and how that impacts the study of galaxy evolution over time. 

Webb, in collaboration with NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, will continue to bring back data that help astronomers gain a deeper understanding of our universe. 

Credits: STScI, D. Kirshenblat; Many thanks to: Dr. Danielle Berg, Dr. Bethan James, Dr. Harkey Katz, Dr. Peter Senchyna, Dr. Piyush Sharda, & Dr. Liz Tarantino

Light up the night 🔥

The spiral galaxy NGC 1385 glows with regions where stars are actively forming.

@NASAChandraXray data (magenta) highlights stellar nurseries and X-ray binaries (like a black hole, neutron star, or white dwarf pulling material from a companion star).

@NASAHubble's optical (white and gray) and @NASAWebb's infrared (orange and red) observations showcase the galaxy's dusty spiral structures.

These multiwavelength observations help scientists learn how nearby galaxies with active star formation build up mass over time.

caption.text:
Webb and the Case of the Mysterious Radio Bursts from Outer Space 🔎

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) - enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe - were discovered in 2007.  Because most flash only once, their origins are difficult to pinpoint, but Webb has found a galaxy that is host to the most distant FRB seen to date.

Originally detected in 2024 by a radio telescope called MeerKAT, its location was known, but ground-based telescopes weren’t sensitive enough to see the galaxy from which it originated. Webb detected the galaxy, and determined how far away it is and how long its light has been traveling towards us. This galaxy existed when the universe was 3 billion years old; the vast majority of FRB occurred billions of years after that.

The FRB’s host galaxy is also atypical - most are massive star-forming galaxies but this one, though actively forming stars, is a dwarf galaxy, about 1000 times less massive than expected. This galaxy existed at a time in the universe’s history where star formation was at its peak - which may be a clue as to what causes FRBs. 

One theory is that FRBs occur when two neutron stars merge - but generally it takes billions of years for orbiting neutron stars to finally spiral into each other, pointing to FRBs being associated with older host galaxies. It’s unlikely this FRB was produced from such a merger.

Another theory is that FRBs can come from a single, extremely magnetic neutron star (a magnetar) having a “starquake.” Because neutron stars are the result of a high-mass star exploding, an FRB could indeed happen on a much shorter timescale, and be found in younger galaxies just like this dwarf one.

Fun fact: FRBs are like cosmic flashlights, illuminating everything along their paths, revealing matter and structures previously hidden from us. In this case, the imprint of two cosmic structures - the nearby Virgo Cluster, as well as a previously unknown galaxy cluster located 3.5 billion light years away from Earth. 

Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, T. Nanayakkara (University of Sydney). Image Processing: J. DePasquale (STScI)

caption.text:
Warning: These slides may cause existential wonder ✨To celebrate World Space Week, today’s #GoogleDoodle spotlights a never-before-seen photo of the Rosebud Nebula – a cosmic stellar nursery located 3,300 light-years away, captured by the James Webb Telescope.  

Keep swiping for distant planets and cosmic phenomena, along with answers to a few of the millions of questions they spark  🌌

what is cosmic dust and how is it so thick|

Cosmic dust is a collection of tiny solid particles – microscopic grains of carbon, silicates, and ice – that float through outer space. Although they appear remarkably thick and solid, their apparent density is an illusion caused by immense scale.

Explore more with Google Search

why is jupiter’s north pole glowing electric blue|
 
Jupiter’s north pole glows electric blue because of a gigantic, permanent ultraviolet aurora caused by high-energy particles, gas excitation, and volcanic power.

what are the clouds in the carina nebula made of|

The clouds in the Carina Nebula are made of molecular gas and cosmic dust, with the main components being hydrogen, smaller amounts of ionized elements like oxygen, sulfur, and nitrogen – which give the nebula its colorful glow – and tiny grains of heavier elements like carbon and silicates.

how far away is our closest giant galactic neighbor, andromeda, and is it true it’s heading toward us| 

The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away from us, and it is indeed heading straight toward the Milky Way. Traveling at roughly 68 to 110 miles per second (110–180 km/s), the galaxies will collide and merge in about 4 to 4.5 billion years.

what are the massive bubbles that appear in space|

Massive bubbles in space are giant cavities or shells of hot, superthin gas carved out by exploding stars, stellar winds, or outbursts from supermassive black holes.

how can an ancient star cluster be made of “heavy metal”|

In astronomy,”‘metal” refers to any element heavier than hydrogen and helium, meaning even common elements like carbon or oxygen are technically called metals. An ancient star cluster can contain these heavier elements because earlier generations of massive stars forged them in

caption.text:
Brewing up new stars 🪄
 
@NASAWebb’s unique view of the stellar nursery known as NGC 7129 reveals numerous stars formerly hidden in this cosmic cauldron. 
 
Stars begin their life in cold, dense regions of dust and gas, hiding from view of most telescopes. Webb’s high degree of infrared sensitivity allows astronomers to peer through dust to study these baby stars. 
 
In this image, we can see stars in various stages of development. The most mature and massive (about 5-8x the mass of our Sun) is the region’s bright central star. In the cavity on the left, appearing in gold, is the largest demonstration of its impact. The outflows from an earlier stage in the star’s development carve into the dense molecular cloud of hydrogen, and combine with the star’s light, causing it to glow. 
 
The region on the right, represented in red, hides much younger objects than those on the left: protostars. As the protostars accumulate matter and increase mass, they eject outflows of super heated material that interact with matter around the star, creating shocks that cause the textured appearance we see in this image. More protostar outflows are at upper left where a dark shadow is being cast by a protostar disk, visible against the surrounding nebula, depicted in blue. 
 
Seeing these different structures help astronomers study the star lifecycle in various stages, leading to a more complete understanding of our universe. 

See more in the link in @NASAWebb’s bio.
 
Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Processing: Alyssa Pagan.

caption.text:
They say planet formation’s a cruel endeavor

Violent collisions, like that between a proto-Earth and a Mars-sized object named Theia 4.5 billion years ago, shaped our home planet. Webb is helping us compare other young stellar systems to the history of our own.

As a star ages, the environment surrounding it changes. The material in its gas-rich protoplanetary disk form planetesimals, which can then combine and break apart to create planets and moons, eventually leaving a gas-poor disk of leftover debris. These debris disks are analogs to the debris in our own solar system, namely our asteroid belt and Kuiper belt. 

Some stars have large amounts of warm dust close-in, that are very bright in the infrared - a rare subclass called “extreme debris disks.” The retired infrared Spitzer Space Telescope discovered these objects, and Webb took a closer look using its powerful infrared sensitivity. Webb confirmed several key things: that extreme debris disks have smaller dust grains than in protoplanetary or classic debris disks; a high concentration of warm dust; and vary irregularly in brightness. 

Some of these disks are rich in silica and some are poor, and which  category an extreme debris disk belongs to speaks to the type of collisions that produced the debris. Silica-rich disks seem to be produced by high-energy impacts between Mars-sized bodies around younger stars. Silica-poor ones might be formed by smaller scale collisions across a range of ages, and often show greater variability in their brightness, probably due to how the debris is being produced by multiple impacts.

Bringing this back to home, our own solar system might have experienced more than one extreme debris disk phase, like when the Earth, with its silica-rich crust was formed by a giant collision. The gas giants migrating outward may have disrupted smaller bodies, generating the dust-rich conditions we observe in extreme debris disks. Understanding how our rocky planets formed and how the giant planets evolved help us to bring the bigger picture into clearer view.

Read more at the link in our bio. 

Image credit: Illustration: NASA, ESA, CSA, Joseph Olmsted (STScI)

Watch out, these non-besties are all across the universe!  If your bestie: is an old soul, gives off dark and mysterious vibes, always seems hungry… That’s not your bestie, that’s an early universe black hole.

Image: An image of many glowing galaxies in various shapes and colours, including spiral and elliptical galaxies, on a black background. A small yellow box near the top of this image highlights a small collection of galaxies. A yellow arrow points to black hole CANUCS-LRD-z8.6 in MACS J1149.5+2223. It existed just 570 million years after the big bang. 

Image credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, G. Rihtaršič (University of Ljubljana, FMF), R. Tripodi (University of Ljubljana, FMF)

Watch out, these non-besties are all across the universe!  If your bestie: runs rings around you, has a lot of energy, isn’t quite what they appear to be… That’s not your bestie, that’s a planetary nebula.
 Image: Planetary Nebula NGC 1514. Two central bright stars shine with bright purple diffraction spikes at the center of a large, diffuse cylinder of gas and dust that is tipped to the right. At the center is a bright pink clumpy cloud that takes up about 25% of the view. The pink region has some holes and diffuse areas. Beyond that are two large rings seen at a roughly 60-degree angle that appear joined at top left and bottom right. The rings appear orange at top left and bottom right, and are blue at bottom and center right.   Image credits: Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, NASA-JPL, Caltech, UCLA, Michael Ressler (NASA-JPL), Dave Jones (IAC)

Watch out, these non-besties are all across the universe!

If your bestie: thrives on shock value, has a dark streak, enjoys K-pop… That’s not your bestie, that’s a protostar.  Image:  A close-in image of a protoplanetary disc around a newly formed star. Many different wavelengths of light are combined and represented by separate and various colors. A dark line across the center is the disc, made of opaque dust: the star is hidden in here and creates a strong glow in the center. A band going straight up is a jet, while other outflows form flares above and below the disc, and a tail coming off to one side.

caption.text:
Seeing double… or quadruple! 

In this Webb image of galaxy cluster MACS J0454.1-0300, we can see the brilliant golden galaxies that make up the cluster and several orange galaxies clustered on one side of the image. The orange galaxies are not part of the galaxy cluster, but rather galaxies much farther away whose light has been bent and magnified by gravitational lensing. This phenomenon occurs when the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. 

In addition to making galaxies look stretched out or bent, gravitational lensing can also make us see double — or quadruple. Under certain conditions, multiple images of the same galaxy can appear. It’s rare to see four or more images of the same galaxy, as this requires the position of the background object and the shape of the massive foreground object to be just so. This happened twice in this image of MACS J0454.1-0300, marking the first time researchers have spotted this more than once in the same galaxy cluster. 

In the second slide, @NASAHubble’s 2014 image of galaxy cluster MACS J0454.1-0300 shows quite a different scene. Because Webb is more sensitive to redder light, we are able to see hundreds more galaxies in the same scene.

Image Descriptions:
1: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the center. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's center; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in color; bright, nearby stars are the same color.

2: A Hubble Space Telescope image of a galaxy cluster. Three large, white stars are seen with four diffraction spikes and hundreds of golden galaxies scattered against the black background of space.

caption.text:
Together, NASA's telescopes wear many hats – capturing different wavelengths of light and cosmic happenings.

This group image of the Sombrero Galaxy shows how! Hubble's visible-light vision highlights the glow of the galaxy's center (warm white), while @NASAChandraXray isolates point sources and hot gas in the galactic halo (cyan and orange). Plus, @NASAWebb's infrared data brings out dust lanes (purple-red).

Also known as M104, this spiral galaxy shines about 28 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

Image description: M104 has a wide, flat, round brim, shown here as a hazy violet ring viewed nearly on its edge. At the center of the brim-like ring is a cluster of golden specks surrounding a warm white core.

Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/SAO; Optical:NASA/Hubble Heritage Team/AURA/STScI; Infrared: NASA/ESA/CSA/STScI; Image Processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/L. Frattare

caption.text:
We see a brand new day dawning 🦋

We’re celebrating the launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope with a little Dolly Parton. Both appreciated the light of a clear blue morning, like the telescope launched into.

This observatory joins our eyes like @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb observing the long dark night of our universe. Roman will explore even further into the unseen in dark energy and dark matter. With our fleet of explorers studying the universe, everything’s gonna be alright.

 As the telescope travels to its new home 1 million miles away from Earth, its instruments will keep turning on and preparing to bring us the light of a brand-new day.

node.accessibility_caption: Photo by NASA Webb Telescope on September 15, 2026. May be an image of text.

caption.text:
In a class of their own

Hidden within this star-forming nebula (captured by our Webb telescope in one of its largest images to date) are strange objects called brown dwarfs. Generally less massive than stars and more massive than planets, they are neither. They form the same way stars do, but they never quite "ignite." Just how small are the smallest objects created by the star-formation process?
 
The brown dwarfs here are about twice the mass of Jupiter - the least massive brown dwarfs found to date. For comparison, brown dwarfs are typically around 13 to 80 times Jupiter’s mass. These are so small, their existence poses challenges to the theories of star formation.

Adding to their strangeness, one of these showed signs of a disk, suggesting small planets could form around an object that itself is only the mass of a planet.

Read more at the link in @NASAWebb’s bio. See comments for image description. 

Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Kevin Luhman (PSU), Catarina Alves de Oliveira (ESA), Mahdi Zamani (ESA/Webb)
